summary: Find the longest subarray in which no value appears more than k times.
mainInsight: Expand right; only the newly added value can break the condition, so while its count exceeds k move the left edge forward (decrementing counts) until it is back to k.

approaches.name: Sliding window with counts
approaches.summary: Count each value in the window; shrink while cnt[nums[r]] > k.

promptVariants: Which pattern solves 'longest subarray where every count <= k'?
What validity check does the window need?
options: Sliding window with a frequency map
Sorting + binary search over the sorted array
Monotonic stack of the element counts so far
Prefix sums over the element counts directly
cards.answer: Sliding window with a frequency map
cards.explanation: Counts only change by one element per step, so validity is easy to maintain.

promptVariants: Why is it enough to check only cnt[nums[r]] after adding nums[r]?
Why can't any other value be the violator?
cards.answer: Before adding nums[r] the window was valid (all counts <= k). Adding one element only increases that element's count, so only nums[r] can exceed k. Shrinking until its count is <= k restores validity.
keyPoints: Only the new value's count changes
cards.explanation: That makes validity an O(1) check.
Each index is added and removed once.

promptVariants: What is the space complexity of the count map?
Why can the count map grow to O(n) in this problem while it stayed constant in Fruit Into Baskets?
cards.answer: O(n) in the worst case (all values distinct), or O(min(n, number of distinct values)).
keyPoints: One key per distinct value in the window
cards.explanation: Unlike Fruit Into Baskets, the number of keys is not bounded by a constant.

promptVariants: Why is the shrink condition `cnt[nums[r]] > k` instead of checking all counts?
What does popping zero-count keys accomplish here?
cards.code:
cnt[nums[r]] += 1
while cnt[nums[r]] > k:
    cnt[nums[l]] -= 1
    if cnt[nums[l]] <= 0:
        cnt.pop(nums[l])
    l += 1
best = max(best, r - l + 1)
cards.answer: Only the value just added can violate the limit, so a single comparison suffices; the loop removes elements from the left (possibly other values) until one copy of nums[r] has left. Popping zero-count keys is optional here (they are never inspected via len), it only keeps the map small.
keyPoints: Only the new value can violate
cards.explanation: In 'at most k distinct' the pop is mandatory because len(map) is the metric.

promptVariants: What is the answer for [6,1,6,1,6,2,6], k = 2?
How long is the longest valid window?
cards.explanation: The window [1,6,1,6,2] keeps every value at most twice; extending it left or right adds a third 6.

incorrectOptionExplanations.7: The whole array has four 6s, so it breaks the limit of 2.
incorrectOptionExplanations.4: A valid window of length 5 exists.
